title: Garland v. Cargill (2024)
summary: A semiautomatic rifle fitted with a bump stock is not a “machinegun” under 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b): each round follows a separate function of the trigger, which must release and reset between shots, and continued fire depends on the shooter’s sustained forward pressure rather than occurring automatically, so ATF’s 2018 rule exceeded its statutory authority.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 2024. Key line: A bump stock does not convert a semiautomatic rifle into a machinegun any more than a shooter with a lightning-fast trigger finger does. (Justice Thomas)

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Attorney General Merrick Garland and the federal officials responsible for ATF, defending the agency’s 2018 bump-stock rule. The respondent was Michael Cargill, who owned two bump stocks, surrendered them under protest, and sued under the Administrative Procedure Act. Justice Thomas wrote for a 6–3 Court on June 14, 2024; Justice Alito concurred; Justice Sotomayor dissented, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson.
sections.Material Facts: The National Firearms Act of 1934 defines a machinegun as a weapon that “shoots, is designed to shoot, or can be readily restored to shoot, automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger.” Bump firing uses recoil to speed that cycle: the shooter holds the trigger finger stationary and pushes the rifle forward, so recoil releases the trigger and forward pressure bumps it back into the finger. A bump stock replaces the rifle’s rear stock with a sliding casing and a ledge for the trigger finger. On more than ten occasions ATF had concluded that bump-stock rifles were not machineguns. After a gunman using bump-stock rifles killed fifty-eight people at a Las Vegas festival in October 2017, bills to ban the devices stalled, and ATF reversed course in a 2018 rule that required owners to destroy or surrender the devices within ninety days.
sections.Procedural History: Cargill surrendered two bump stocks under protest and sued under the APA, alleging that ATF exceeded its statutory authority because the devices fall outside § 5845(b). After a bench trial the Western District of Texas entered judgment for ATF, 502 F. Supp. 3d 1163, and a Fifth Circuit panel affirmed, 20 F.4th 1004. On rehearing en banc the Fifth Circuit reversed, 57 F.4th 447: a majority found the statute at least ambiguous and applied the rule of lenity for Cargill, while an eight-judge plurality read it as unambiguously excluding bump-stock rifles. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a circuit split, heard argument on February 28, 2024, and affirmed.
sections.Issue: Does a bump stock convert a semiautomatic rifle into a “machinegun” under § 5845(b) by enabling it to shoot automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger? The answer turns on two phrases: whether each shot from a bump-stock rifle results from a separate “function of the trigger,” and whether the weapon fires “automatically” when the shooter must keep the right forward pressure on the front grip with the nontrigger hand.
sections.Holding: No, on both grounds. A bump-stock-equipped semiautomatic rifle does not fire more than one shot by a single function of the trigger, because the trigger must release and reset between shots and each bump of the trigger against the stationary finger is a separate function; the bump stock only shortens the time between functions. Even if it fired more than one shot per function, it would not do so automatically, because the shooter must supply continuing manual input by maintaining forward pressure on the front grip, a single function of the trigger “and then some.” ATF therefore exceeded its statutory authority, and the en banc Fifth Circuit’s judgment for Cargill was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Contemporary dictionaries defined “function” as the mode of action by which a thing fulfills its purpose and “trigger” as the lever that activates a mechanism, so “function of the trigger” is the physical trigger movement that fires the weapon. Diagrams of the AR-15’s trigger, hammer and disconnector showed that one engagement fires one cartridge; a later shot requires a new engagement, with or without a bump stock. ATF’s own definition undercut it: the rule defined a function as a pull “and analogous motions,” and ATF conceded that sliding the rifle forward to bump the trigger is such a motion, so each bump is its own function. On “automatically,” the syntax requires the single trigger function itself to cause more than one shot, but bump fire also requires the nontrigger hand to maintain calibrated forward pressure. ATF’s treatment of the Ithaca Model 37 shotgun confirmed the line: holding its trigger while pumping produces multiple shots, yet ATF classifies it outside the definition because the pump supplies manual input. The presumption against ineffectiveness failed because the statute still reaches traditional machineguns.

topics.lrs-k-textualism: The majority resolves the case on dictionary definitions and the mechanics of the trigger and refuses to rewrite the text to serve a broader purpose that Congress did not enact.
topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: The dissent relies on the NRA president's 1934 hearing testimony and the House and Senate Reports as evidence of contemporaneous meaning, while the majority decides without them.
topics.lrs-k-purposivism: The dissent's presumption against ineffectiveness argues that a text's manifest purpose must not be defeated by easy evasion; the majority answers that a law is not useless because it draws a line more narrowly than one of its purposes might suggest.
topics.lrs-k-lenity: The en banc Fifth Circuit resolved the ambiguity it found in section 5845(b) in Cargill's favor under the rule of lenity; the Supreme Court found the text clear and did not need lenity.
topics.lrs-o-rulemaking-authority: ATF's Rule reinterpreting a criminal statute, after more than 10 contrary classifications, exceeded the agency's statutory authority, so the challenge under the APA succeeded.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Alito concurred: an M16 and a bump-stock rifle differ little in practice, but the text compels different treatment, and the remedy is legislation, which might already have passed had ATF kept its earlier reading. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, read “single function of the trigger” from the shooter’s perspective as the single human act that starts a firing sequence, relying on 1934 hearing testimony and committee reports equating the phrase with a single pull; a bump-stock shooter initiates fire once and then maintains forward pressure just as an M16 shooter holds the trigger back, and the presumption against ineffectiveness applies because bump stocks fire 400 to 800 rounds a minute.
learning.why: Cargill shows a textualist majority and a textualist dissent reaching opposite results from the same dictionary definitions, and shows how legislative history, contemporaneous usage and the presumption against ineffectiveness are admitted or excluded from the analysis. It also shows a court deciding the limits of an agency's statutory authority without deferring to the agency's reading.
